sources.title: Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld (Q156749), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-06): English label 'Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld', description 'Finland Swedish baron, geologist, mineralogist and Arctic explorer (1832-1901)', Korean label 아돌프 에리크 노르덴스키욀드 (the Korean Wikipedia article is titled 아돌프 에리크 노르덴셸드), born 1832-11-18, died 1901-08-12, citizenship Sweden and the Grand Duchy of Finland. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry 'Nordenskiold, (Nils) Adolf Erik' by George Kish (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full including its bibliography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: first Arctic voyage 1857 (Spitsbergen), five more Spitsbergen voyages and eight other expeditions 1864-86, the Vega voyage of 1878-79 that achieved the Northeast Passage, scientific work made an integral part of Arctic exploration with careful planning, equipment and staff, five Vega volumes that began serious polar studies, chief of mineralogy at the Swedish national museum from 1858, the Facsimile-atlas (1889) and Periplus (1897) as foundations of the history of cartography, and influence on two generations of Scandinavian scientists. Reference-work biography by the author of the standard English biography; admiring, but says his theoretical geology is now only of historical interest.

P. Andrew Karam, 'Baron Nils Adolf Erik Nordenskiold', Science and Its Times (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). COUNTER-VOICE: after the Vega voyage he turned to the history of maps and, in the entry's words, made some significant discoveries but also serious blunders; he accepted maps as authentic too readily, bought several forged maps, based statements on documents later found to be fakes, and attributed to old mapmakers knowledge they could not have had, which reduced his credibility; the entry still concludes that he contributed tremendously. Also: ten voyages 1858-1883, he did not set out to expand an empire, and his Voyage of the Vega was a popular and scientific narrative translated into several languages. Secondary encyclopaedia entry with no cited instances beyond the map errors.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Adolf Erik, Baron Nordenskiöld' (revised November 2025; read in full): settled in Stockholm in 1858, curator of mineralogy at the Swedish State Museum, led Spitsbergen expeditions in 1864, 1868 and 1872-73, a Greenland inland-ice expedition in 1870, preliminary Kara Sea voyages in 1875 and 1876, then the Vega (sailed 21 July 1878, frozen in near the Bering Strait from late September to 18 July 1879, reached Stockholm 24 April 1880 and was created a baron); in 1883 he penetrated far into the Greenland ice and is said to be the first to break through the southeast Greenland sea-ice barrier. Short reference article; celebratory, no criticism.

Robert MacDonald, 'Arctic Profiles: Nils Adolf Erik Nordenskiold (1832-1901)', Arctic (journal of the Arctic Institute of North America, University of Calgary), pp. 388-389 (two-page PDF read in full; volume and year are not printed on the extract). Independent polar-research profile: eight further Arctic trips besides the Vega; he chose scientists from across Scandinavia, many of whom sailed with him again; the 1872-73 winter expedition (backed by businessmen hoping to exploit phosphate deposits) in which ice and a storm scattered the reindeer meant for the Pole march and a failed relief left 67 men on supplies for 25 in a prefabricated hut; the 1875 Yenisei journey; Vega preparations including study of earlier voyage records; Sami skiers on the 1883 Greenland ice cap; later life as museum administrator, author of the Facsimile Atlas and adviser to Nansen's Greenland crossing. Includes a candid account of the hardships and of commercial backing.

National Library of Finland (Helsinki University Library): Maire Aho, 'A. E. Nordenskiold Collection included in the Unesco Memory of the World Program', Tietolinja News 1/1999, and the Library's 'A. E. Nordenskiöld Collection' collection page (both read in full). He was 'very orderly' in acquiring maps, spending the royalties of his Vega narrative on books and maps and using other works as exchange material; the collection holds about 4,000 titles and 24,000 maps (an almost complete Ptolemy series, 123 incunabula), was inscribed in UNESCO Memory of the World in 1997, and passed to Helsinki in 1902 only because no buyer was found abroad or in Sweden; the sale terms kept it whole and open to scholars from any country. The Aho article also names his three financial guarantors for the Vega (King Oscar II, Oscar Dickson, Alexander Sibiryakov) and says the long stay in the ice yielded data of a quality not matched until the 1930s. Institutional, admiring.

Urban Wrakberg, 'A. E. Nordenskiöld in Swedish memory: the origin and uses of Arctic heroism', Acta Borealia 36(2), 2019 (only the abstract was read, via the British Library catalogue record; the full article was not available). CRITICAL FRAMING: polar heroes were built for national honour and youth education; Nordenskiöld, with the help of others, navigated the drift ice, the international republic of science and the Swedish, Finnish and Russian national scenes and was turned into a national hero in Finland and Sweden. Used only to bound hero-narrative claims, not as behavioural evidence.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_britannica, src_nordenskiold_nlf, src_nordenskiold_arctic | 1857-1897 | reference biographies, institutional collection page, polar profile] Documented output in several unrelated fields: mineralogy and geology (chief of the mineralogy division from 1858), Arctic expeditions, a fundamental work on the chemist Scheele and on eighteenth-century Swedish science, and the history of cartography with the Facsimile-atlas and Periplus plus a 24,000-map collection (DSB, NLF). Four source types agree. The counter-voice entry says the cartographic turn brought serious errors, which concerns quality rather than range.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_arctic, src_nordenskiold_nlf, src_nordenskiold_britannica | 1868-1880 | reference biography, polar profile, institutional article, reference article] The DSB says his expeditions were distinguished by careful planning, meticulously prepared scientific equipment and a qualified staff; the polar profile and the library article say he studied earlier voyage records and Norwegian fishermen's logs, and the Britannica article lists the preliminary Kara Sea voyages of 1875 and 1876 before the Vega. Against this, the polar profile records the 1872-73 winter in which reindeer were scattered and 67 men lived on supplies for 25 after a failed relief, and the Vega was frozen in for ten months. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 76 / 0.66 to 72 / 0.62 and impact set to dual-edged because a documented 1872-73 supply shortfall is a counterexample the admiring sources do not weigh.

persistence.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_britannica, src_nordenskiold_arctic | 1857-1883 | reference biography, reference article, polar profile] Repeated Arctic campaigns across 26 years: five more Spitsbergen voyages and eight other expeditions after 1857 (DSB), the Greenland expeditions of 1870 and 1883, a winter in Spitsbergen in 1872-73 after a failed pole attempt, and the Vega's ten months in the ice before completing the passage (Britannica, polar profile). Several of the expeditions did not reach their stated goals and he returned to the field each time.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_britannica, src_nordenskiold_nlf | 1864-1880 | reference biography, reference article, institutional article] He led his own expeditions to Spitsbergen from 1864, to Greenland in 1870 and 1883 and commanded the Vega expedition, a thirty-man crew with ships supplied by three financial guarantors (DSB, Britannica, NLF). Documentation concerns holding command repeatedly; sources say little on how he sought or exercised it day to day.

collaboration.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_arctic | 1861-1880 | reference biography, polar profile] The polar profile says he chose scientists from across Scandinavia, many of whom sailed with him again, and the DSB says he selected a well-qualified staff and offered two generations of Scandinavian scientists field experience and generous support; the Vega results were published as a five-volume multi-discipline report. Both sources are admiring and neither narrates a specific disagreement, so the score stays moderate. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): collaboration lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 66 / 0.52 because two sources only (a polar profile and the DSB), both retrospective and admiring.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_nlf, src_nordenskiold_dsb | 1878-1897 | institutional article, reference biography] The library article calls him 'very orderly' in acquiring maps, which it gives as the reason for the collection's exceptional quality (24,000 maps, a nearly complete series of Ptolemy editions), and the DSB notes meticulous preparation of scientific equipment and the Facsimile-atlas as a careful survey. Offset by the counter-voice entry, which says he too readily accepted forged maps, so the care was real but not error-proof. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): detail_orientation lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.5 because rests on one library article calling him orderly in acquiring maps.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_scitimes | 1889-1897 | reference biography, counter-voice encyclopaedia entry] The two reference works conflict: the DSB says he was the first to apply the critical approach of the historian to the history of cartography, whereas the Science and Its Times entry says he accepted maps as authentic too readily, bought several forged maps, based statements on documents later shown to be fake and over-read the knowledge of old mapmakers. Neither gives a fully cited case, so the score sits near the middle with low confidence and a dual-edged impact.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_arctic, src_nordenskiold_britannica | 1872-1879 | polar profile, reference article] He wintered 67 men on supplies for 25 in 1872-73 after the relief failed, and the Vega, sailing close to the Siberian coast, was frozen in for roughly ten months near the Bering Strait before the passage was completed; he nonetheless led further expeditions. The sources document exposure to danger but not his own weighing of the risk, so this is a low-confidence inference and not a high score.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_nlf, src_nordenskiold_arctic, src_nordenskiold_dsb | 1858-1878 | institutional article, polar profile, reference biography] He secured the King, Oscar Dickson and Alexander Sibiryakov as financial guarantors for the Vega (NLF); businessmen backed the 1872-73 voyage hoping for phosphate deposits and Dickson's money spurred government aid (polar profile); the DSB says he was persuasive in urging others to report their findings. The financing outcomes are documented but how he persuaded is not. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.48 because the trait is inferred from patrons' funding decisions and one general DSB phrase, not from any described act of persuasion.

curiosity.rationale: [src_nordenskiold_dsb, src_nordenskiold_nlf | 1850s-1890s | reference biography, institutional article] The DSB says he was interested in eighteenth-century Swedish science from an early age and that his preparation for Arctic voyages led him into old maps, which became a main interest; the library article dates his map interest to the Spitsbergen expeditions and says he spent the royalties of his Vega book on books and maps. Documented sustained interest across mineralogy, polar nature and cartographic history; the early-age claim is a single-source statement.

portrait.source: Albumen carte-de-visite photograph of Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld by the Paris studio of E. Appert (Ernest Charles Appert), dated by the museum between 1860 and 1890, held by the Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris (inventory PH22367, 8.4 x 5.7 cm print on a 10.5 x 6.3 cm mount). The mount is printed 'E. APPERT' and the verso carries the sitter's name handwritten as 'Nordenskyold'. The file is the photograph area cropped from the museum's 1337 x 2160 pixel image and downscaled to 717 x 1200 (no upscaling).
portrait.license: CC0 1.0 as stated on the Paris Musées collections item page for the Musée Carnavalet record (the photographer died in 1890, so the photograph is also old by age)
portrait.attribution: Ernest Charles Appert (photographer), portrait of Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, albumen carte de visite, 1860-1890. Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris, PH22367, CC0 Paris Musées. Cropped and downscaled.
portrait.creator: Ernest Charles Appert (Paris photographic studio of E. Appert)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead-robust) (lead) / CONFIRMED: the lead's Appert photograph was used; the live Paris Musees item page and IIIF manifest were opened (the URL the lead tried returned 404, the correct item URL works) and show CC0, creator Ernest Charles Appert (1831-1890), 1860-1890, carte de visite; I looked at both recto and verso: printed 'E. APPERT' on the mount and handwritten 'Nordenskyold' (ink and pencil) on the verso, no contradiction. The CC0 label is the holder's own; Appert died in 1890 so the photograph is also old by age. KIND likeness (a studio carte de visite of the sitter). The Rosen photograph at the Accademia delle Scienze di Torino and the Stodart engraving from the Vega book were not needed. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-06, Wikidata API) Q156749 label 'Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld', description 'Finland Swedish baron, geologist, mineralogist and Arctic explorer (1832-1901)', ko label 아돌프 에리크 노르덴스키욀드, born 1832-11-18, died 1901-08-12, citizenship Sweden and Grand Duchy of Finland; not in prod66.json and no candidate file or QID collision existed. REGION western_europe: career base Stockholm from 1858 (Swedish National Museum, Swedish expeditions, Swedish baronetcy), Swedish precedents are western_europe; he was born in Helsinki and left Finland in the 1850s. Nationality codes SE and FI. ERA 19th_century. ZERO POLITICS: primary identity is Arctic explorer, mineralogist and historian of cartography; his student-era liberalism and exile from Finland, a 1899 petition to the tsar for the Finnish constitution and the national-hero narrative (Wrakberg) are context only and unscored; no row relies on them. VOCABULARY: occupations explorer and scientist, fields exploration and natural_science, tags explorer, field_researcher, organizer, archetype scientific_explorer, impact domains scientific and historical, all labelled in en.ts and ko.ts (geologist, mineralogist, cartography historian and geography have no label so were not used). KO NAME: Korean Wikipedia article title 아돌프 에리크 노르덴셸드 (standard Korean Wikipedia title; the Wikidata label is a different transliteration). ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive expedition records and reference biographies). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by George Kish on Nordenskiold (https://encyclopedia.com/science/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/nordenskiold-nils-adolf-erik). READ (6 sources besides Wikidata): DSB entry (full); Science and Its Times entry (full, counter-voice); Britannica (full); Arctic Profiles in Arctic (full 2-page PDF); National Library of Finland article by Aho plus the collection page (full); Wrakberg 2019 (abstract only). Wikipedia not used. The publisher blurb for Nils Uddenberg's biography 'The Polar Explorer' was seen only in search snippets and is not used; Kish's 1973 biography, Leslie's 1879 account and Nordenskiold's own Vega narrative were not opened. PERSPECTIVES: (1) scientific reference biography (DSB); (2) science-history encyclopaedia entry with explicit criticism of his cartographic errors; (3) general encyclopaedia (Britannica); (4) independent polar-research profile that records the 1872-73 hardships and commercial backing; (5) library institution on his collecting; (6) historiographic abstract on hero-making. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all of the above; no row rests on his own writings. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: death date 12 August 1901 (Wikidata, DSB, Britannica) versus 2 August in the polar profile (12 August followed); the DSB credits him with the first critical historical approach to cartography whereas the Science and Its Times entry documents forged-map errors (both reflected in analytical_rigor); the DSB dates his first Arctic voyage 1857 whereas Britannica and the polar profile say 1858 (the cards avoid the year); the Vega's winter in the ice is described by the library article as an 'unlucky stay' that was scientifically productive and by Britannica simply as being frozen in. Not an adversarial biography: the two critical voices are the Science and Its Times entry and the polar profile's account of 1872-73. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE (first pass PASS on all five): cards (1) Vega and the Northeast Passage, (2) the Arctic expedition programme with scientific work built in (Spitsbergen, Greenland, five-volume Vega results), (3) the history of cartography and the map collection now in Helsinki. Mineralogy post and the Scheele work stay in rows, not cards. SELF-CALIBRATION: reviewed planning_orientation (lowered 76/0.66 to 72/0.62, impact dual-edged), persuasiveness (lowered 70/0.54 to 66/0.48), cross_domain_range (kept). No broad scoring problem flagged.
